verses.zh: 耶和华的话又临到我说：
verses.en: The Lord’s message came to me:

verses.zh: 「你们在以色列地怎么用这俗语说『父亲吃了酸葡萄，儿子的牙酸倒了』呢？」
verses.en: “What do you mean by quoting this proverb concerning the land of Israel: “‘The fathers eat sour grapes,And the children’s teeth become numb?’[NOTE:1]
notes: This word occurs three times, in the Qal stem here and the parallel passage in Jer 31:29-30, and in the Piel stem at Eccl 10:10. In the latter passage it refers to the bluntness of an ax that has not been sharpened. Here the “bluntness” of the teeth is not due to grinding them down because of the bitter taste of sour grapes but to the fact that they have lost their “edge,” “bite,” or “sharpness” because they are numb from the sour taste. For this meaning for the word, see W. L. Holladay, Jeremiah (Hermeneia), 2:197.

verses.zh: 主耶和华说：「我指着我的永生起誓，你们在以色列中，必不再有用这俗语的因由。
verses.en: “As surely as I live, declares the Sovereign Lord,[NOTE:1] you will not quote this proverb in Israel anymore!

verses.zh: 看哪，世人都是属我的；为父的怎样属我，为子的也照样属我；犯罪的，他必死亡。
verses.en: Indeed! All lives are mine—the life of the father as well as the life of the son is mine. The one[NOTE:1] who sins will die.

verses.zh: 「人若是公义，且行正直与合理的事：
verses.en: “Suppose a man is righteous. He practices what is just and right;

Heb “does not lift up his eyes.” This refers to looking to idols for help.
The expression קָרַב אֶל (qarav ʾel) means “draw near to” or “approach,” but is also used as a euphemism for the intended purpose of sexual relations (Lev 18:14; Deut 22:14; Isa 8:3).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This chapter provides a good opportunity to mention how the interpreter's presuppositions often distort the original
author's intent. As an evangelical I have often used this text as an example of individual, personal response being necessary
for salvation (i.e. personal relationship; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO "RECEIVE," "BELIEVE," "CONFESS/PROFESS," AND "CALL UPON"?). However,
in context, it is referring to Judah's claim that it was because of their ancestors' sins that they were suffering (cf. Exod. 20:5; Deut. 5:9).
This chapter is more related to the current generation (corporate) rather than individuals of that generation.

Another way this chapter is used is seen in Ezek. 18:32. It is often linked with John 3:16; 1 Tim. 2:4; and 2 Pet. 3:9
to show YHWH's love for all humans (which is surely true), but this text is really about Israel's descendants (cf. Ezek. 18:30; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN). We tend to read our
systematic theology into every text. We tend to assign theological content to certain words and then read that definition into every usage
of the term (i.e. "repent," "live"). We must discipline ourselves to let the inspired authors speak to their day before we use it in our systematic
theologies (which often say more about us than about God! see "Bible Interpretation Seminar").

Ezekiel is addressing a sinful people who do not think they are sinful, but rather blame their parents and previous generations for YHWH's judgment.

- This chapter also offers an opportunity to show how biblical authors present truths in tension-filled pairs. Notice how Ezek. 18:31
demands that the believers "make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit," yet Ezek. 36:26-27 asserts that YHWH will give
them a new heart and a new spirit.

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)

There are two ways to view these statements.

- OT

- The first way reflects the first covenant based on human performance (i.e. Deut. 4:1; 5:33; 8:1; 30:16,19).

- The "new" covenant focuses on God's performance (i.e. Ezek. 36:22-36; Jer. 31:31-34).

- NT

- These statements describe a covenant relationship where God initiates (cf. John 6:44,65) and sets the conditions for fellowship.

- Humans must respond initially and continually in repentance and faith (i.e. John 1:12; 3:16; Eph. 2:8-10). Salvation is not a
ticket to heaven or an insurance policy, but a daily personal relationship.

SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord

- Note that the NKJV prints Ezek. 18:4-18 (i.e. Ezek. 18:4-9, 10-13, 14-17,18) as poetry; NIV prints Ezek. 18:5-17
(i.e. Ezek. 18:5-9, 10-13a, 15-17a) as poetry and Ezek. 18:13b-14 as prose, however, the NASB, NRSV, TEV, NJB,
JPSOA, and REB print the whole chapter in prose. It is difficult to identify poetry vs. elevated prose.

- I like the brief outline in the Oxford Study Bible, p. 874.

"Maintaining right relations with God frees one from

- the past of one's parents, Ezek. 18:1-20

- the past of one's own life, Ezek. 18:21-32"

- The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1073, makes a good point that the normal introductory phrase, "the word of the Lord
came to me," is present in 18:1, but not in 19:1. This may mean they should go together as one context.

- the individual's responsibility

- each Judean King's responsibility

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: EZEKIEL 18:1-4

1Then the word of the Lord came to me, saying, 2"What
do you mean by using this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying,

'The fathers eat the sour grapes,

But the children's teeth are set on edge'?

3As I live," declares the Lord God, "you are surely not going to use
this proverb in Israel anymore. 4Behold, all souls are Mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is Mine. The soul who sins will die.
4Behold, all souls are Mine; the soul of the father as well as the soul of the son is Mine. The soul who sins will die."

18:2 "proverb" The use of this word (BDB 605, KB 647) ties this chapter to a unified context
(i.e. chapters 12-18, cf. Ezek. 12:22,23; 14:8; 17:2; 18:2,3).

▣ "The fathers eat the sour grapes,

But the children's teeth are set on edge"

One person's (or generation's) actions affect others. This is uniquely an eastern
viewpoint. Eastern peoples are far more tribal, clan, and family-oriented. One is a member of a group
and lives to serve that group. One's attitudes and actions affect that group. Here are some
biblical examples.

- Adam and Eve affect the whole human family and the earth, Genesis 3; Rom. 5:12-21 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND)

- Parent's sin or faithfulness affects the children, Exod. 20:5-6; 34:7; Deut. 5:9; 7:9; Ezekiel 18

- Achan's sin affects all of Israel and even some Israeli soldiers die because of his sin, Joshua 7

- David sins, but his first son by Bathsheba dies and Israel languishes, 2 Samuel 11-12; Psalm 32, 51

- Jesus' substitutionary, vicarious death on behalf of all humans, Isaiah 53; Mark 10:45; John 1:29;
Rom. 5:18-19; 2 Cor. 5:21.

In this context the current inhabitants of Jerusalem/Judah are blaming their current situation
of being judged by YHWH on the sins of previous generations. YHWH will not let this excuse stand!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

18:3 "As I live" This is an oath based on the covenant name of God, YHWH (cf. Ezek. 5:11; 14:16,18,20;
16:48; 17:16,19; 18:3; 20:3,31,33; 33:11,27; 34:8; 35:6,11). YHWH is the only-living, ever-living God. All life
is derived from Him, belongs to Him, and remains through Him (i.e. "all souls are Mine," Ezek. 18:4). What He swears
will surely come true (cf. Isa. 55:9-11)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.

▣ "you are surely not going to use this proverb in Israel any more" This same proverb is mentioned in Jer. 31:29,
but in the setting of "the last days." This proverb impugns the justice and fairness of God (cf. Jer. 16:20; Lam. 5:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

18:4 "soul" This is not the Greek concept that we have a soul (i.e. divine spark), but the Hebrew concept that we are a soul
(i.e. nephesh, cf. Gen. 2:7). The Hebrew word (BDB 659, KB 711-713) used four times in this verse, describes the life force
(i.e. breath) in both animals and humans (cf. Gen. 1:20-30; 2:7,19; 7:22; Job 34:14-15; Ps. 104:29, 30; 146:4; Eccl. 3:19-21). Humans
are uniquely related to YHWH by His personal formation of them and His breathing life into them (cf. Gen. 2:7), yet they are also creatures
of this planet. We eat, breathe, reproduce just like other animals of this planet. However, we are also created in God's image and likeness
(cf. Gen. 1:26-27). We are a physical and spiritual unity (i.e. Ps. 42:1).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

SPECIAL TOPIC: BODY AND SPIRIT

▣ "all souls are Mine" This is not a theological statement of monotheism (as in Num. 16:22; 27:16;
Isa. 42:5; 57:16). The original author is speaking of the covenant people and particularly of Judah's
royal line (i.e. Hezekiah, Manasseh, and Josiah).

▣ "The soul who sins will die" The emphasis is on individual covenant responsibility (cf.
Ezek. 14:20; Deut. 24:17). Remember it is not "either/or," but "both/and" between individual responsibility
and corporate responsibility. This same tension can be seen between original sin and volitional sin
(cf. Gen. 2:17; Rom. 6:23; see SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE [biblical paradoxes]).
This truth is also seen in Deut. 24:16.

What does "die" (BDB 559, KB 562) mean here? It must be more than physical death! It is
the opposite of true "life" (cf. Ezek. 18:9). There is "life" (BDB 310, KB 309) beyond this reality.
This "life" is characterized by the presence and character of God.

One wonders how the Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE "sins,"
should be understood. Does it imply that a one-time sin brings death or is that already a reality in
the Fall (cf. Genesis 3; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND)? How would one relate this statement to 1 John 3:6,9
(PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVE)? Are we speaking of sin that characterizes
the life or acts of sin? I would assume, because of the idolatrous actions of Ezek. 18:7 and the
covenant partners' violations of Ezek. 18:8, that we are speaking of a life characterized by covenant
rebellion (cf. Ezek. 18:9).

The Bible mentions three kinds of death or possibly progressive stages of death.
The first is Genesis 3. Adam and Eve ate of the forbidden fruit, but they were still alive physically.
The "death" referred to was relational (i.e. God to human, human to human, and human to self),
as well as contextual (i.e. the planet, the ethos was altered).

The second aspect of death is personal, physical death (cf. Genesis 5). Spiritual death
(cf. Eph. 2:1) resulted in the physical cessation of life.

The third aspect (or progress) is ultimate, everlasting death (cf. Rev. 2:11; 20:6,14),
which involves

- a permanent separation from fellowship with God

- a permanent isolation from God's purpose for creation (i.e. loss of heaven)

- a permanent fellowship of punishment with evil persons and rebellious angels (i.e. Isa. 14:9-20)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHMENT

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?

18:5-9 Notice the characteristics of a righteous covenant follower.

- practices justice (lit. "what is lawful," BDB 1048), Ezek. 18:5

- practices righteousness (lit. "what is right," BDB 842), Ezek. 18:5

cf. Ezek. 6:13), Ezek. 18:6

- does not lift up his eyes to the idols, Ezek. 18:6, cf. Ezek. 18:12,15; 20:24; 33:25; Deut. 4:19
(this denotes looking to them for favors and answers to prayers)

- does not defile his neighbor's wife, Ezek. 18:6, cf. Ezek. 18:15; 22:11; 33:26; Exod. 20:14;
Lev. 18:20; 20:10; Deut. 5:18

- does not have sex with a woman during her menstrual period, Ezek. 18:6, cf. Ezek. 22:10; Lev. 15:19,20,24,25

- does not oppress anyone, Ezek. 18:7, cf. Ezek. 18:12,16; 22:7,29; Exod. 20:21; Lev. 19:33; 25:14,17;
Deut. 23:16

- does not commit robbery, Ezek. 18:7, cf. Lev. 19:13 (e.g. the rich exploiting the poor, Isa. 3:14; 10:2; Micah 2:2)

- gives his bread to the hungry, Ezek. 18:7, cf. Ezek. 18:16; Deut. 15:11

- covers the naked with clothing, Ezek. 18:7, cf. Isa. 58:7; Matt. 25:35; Luke 3:11

Notice some of these are prohibitions and some are mandated actions; some deal with ceremonial
issues, others with sins against a covenant brother. They reflect the Mosaic Covenant.

18:5 "practices justice and righteousness" These two often appear together in describing the person
who lives pleasing to God (cf. 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kgs. 10:9; 1 Chr. 18:14; 2 Chr. 9:8; Ps. 99:4; Isa. 9:7;
32:16; 33:5; 59:14; Jer. 4:2; 9:24; 22:3,15; 23:5; 33:15; Ezek. 18:5,19,21,27; 33:14,16,19; 45:9;
Amos 5:7,24). Pleasing God involves the inner life (heart, mind) and the outer life (worship, ethical
actions, compassion). These cannot be divided. Faith permeates all of life! It is not an isolated ritual,
liturgy, or worship time, but a daily, personal relationship! We must not separate justification from sanctification!

18:7 "restores to the debtor his pledge" Often a poor person's outer cloak was used as collateral for a

Amos 2:8), but land owners often kept it to insure the laborer would return to work the next day.

▣ "does not commit robbery" This refers to the rich landowners taking advantage of the
poor people of the land (cf. Ezek. 18:18:7,12,16; 22:7,29; 45:8; 46:18; Exod. 22:21; Lev. 19:13; Jer. 22:3). They
loaned them money and when they could not pay, they took their land (i.e. God's inheritance to tribes and families from Joshua 12-19).

▣ "gives bread to the hungry and covers the naked with clothing" YHWH cares for the underprivileged and socially
powerless (i.e. widow, orphan, alien); those who know God will also (cf. Deut. 15:11; Isa. 58:7; Matt. 25:31-45; James 2:15-16). Biblical
faith has both a private, internal aspect and an outward, daily living aspect.

18:8 "does not lend money on interest" This was forbidden to fellow Israelites, but permitted to foreigners (cf. Ezek. 18:13,17;
22:12; Exod. 22:25; Lev. 25:35-38; Deut 23:19-20; Ps. 15:5). To be sure, this is mostly an issue of the heart! One's attitude and actions toward
the needy are the focus of these verses (i.e. NT book of James).

True and complete obedience is not a possibility for fallen humanity (cf. Gen. 6:5,11-12; Ps. 14:3; Isa. 53:6; Rom. 1:18-3:20; 5:12-14). Covenant
obedience was the criteria for "a ceremonial righteousness" within ancient Israel. Even in the
Judaism of Jesus' day "righteousness" was defined as

- prayer

- fasting (cf. Matt. 6:1-18, see SPECIAL TOPIC: FASTING)

This chapter is an allusion to the transgenerational communication of sin through families
(cf. Exod. 20:5; Deut. 5:9). However, it also alludes to the gracious character of YHWH (cf. Deut. 5:10; 7:9). The
mercy of God vs. the judgment of God can be compared to judgment, 3-4 generations but mercy to a 1,000
generations! But Ezekiel even removes the 3-4! Each human created in God's image and likeness will stand
before God as an individual based on his/her actions and motives (i.e. Deut. 24:16).

Notice that "the wicked" is parallel with "anyone" in Ezek. 18:32. Contextually this
must refer to covenant people (i.e. here, Judeans), but the OT inclusion of

- non-Israelites such as Job, Melchizedek, Caleb, and Ninevites

- the Mosaic covenant's concern for the resident alien

- Isaiah's revelations of YHWH's love for and inclusion of "the nations" (i.e. Isa. 66:23),
causes one to expand the reference to all humans, which is surely the focus of the "New Covenant" (i.e. John 1:12;
3:16; 4:42; Rom. 11:32; 1 Tim. 2:4; 4:10; Titus 2:11; Heb. 2:9; 2 Pet. 3:9; 1 John 2:1; 4:14).

The Mosaic Covenant is a performance-based, conditional covenant! The question remains, is the NT a conditional covenant?
NT acceptance by God is not performance-based, but the goal of both the OT and NT is a righteous people who reflect God's character to a
lost world! The problem of "easy believism" is the issue. We must not separate justification from sanctification! The NT is a conditional covenant, which requires

- repentance

- faith, trust, belief

- obedience

- perseverance

- service

- worship

The fallen nature which characterizes the OT is matched by the indwelling Spirit of the NT.
This is the newness of Jer. 31:31-34 (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36). The rabbinical proverb, "in every person's heart are two dogs
(black and while). The one you feed most (i.e. yetzer) becomes the biggest" (parapahrase).

I have come to believe that Adam and Eve were not created immortal. Their exclusion from the Garden, where
they had access to the tree of life, is the first clue. Only YHWH has life. He is the ever-living, only-living Being.

In the NT only believers in Jesus are said to have eternal life. This theological understandiing is called
"limited immortality." It surely affects the theology of "eternal punishment" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: ETERNAL PUNISHENT).

This whole area of theology has been unfortunately affected by Greek thought (i.e. every person has a divine spark).
Biblically speaking, humans do not have a soul; they are a soul (i.e. Gen. 2:7).

18:31 It is obvious that even with YHWH's available revelation and mercy, some covenant people will not return to Him.
Some never knew Him. There are two inseparable ways this "knowledge" is manifest.

- personal faith (cf. Gen. 15:6)

One more theological point on these verses. Israel's physical condition was related to
her spiritual condition. Israel's problems were related to her disobedience to YHWH, not YHWH's
weakness related to the other national gods (i.e. Babylonian Marduk). This truth emphasizes the
tension between a sovereign monotheistic Deity and a covenant people with true free will! Israel
reaped the consequences of her choices, not YHWH's (i.e. Ezek. 18:23,32)!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible
for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and
the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Why is this chapter so important in understanding the OT?

- Are we affected by the sins of others? How? Can we be corporately guilty for our society?

- Does God love all humans or just a chosen group?

- What spiritual principle is mentioned in Ezek. 18:30?
